claim: Our solar system is one of over [500] known solar systems in the entire Milky Way galaxy [00:00]
quote: one of over 500 known solar systems in the entire Milky Way galaxy
evidence: Technically true but badly outdated: 'over 500' was roughly the confirmed exoplanet-system count around 2012-2013. By the video's own May 2023 publish date NASA's archive already listed ~5,400 confirmed exoplanets across thousands of systems; the current tally (2026) is 6,416 planets in 4,809 systems, 1,061 of them multi-planet. 'Over 500' undercounts the real figure by roughly 8-10x, which reads as false scarcity rather than the actual abundance.

claim: The solar system formed about [4.5 billion years ago] when a collapsing cloud of interstellar gas and dust formed a solar nebula [00:00]
quote: about 4.5 billion years ago when a cloud of interstellar gas and dust collapsed, resulting in a solar nebula
evidence: NASA: the Sun formed about 4.6 billion years ago from the collapse of the solar nebula, a spinning cloud of gas and dust. 4.5 vs 4.6 billion years is standard rounding, and the nebular-collapse mechanism matches the claim.

claim: The solar system is located in the Milky Way's [Orion star cluster] [00:00]
quote: located in the Milkyways Orion star cluster
evidence: The Sun sits in the Orion Arm (Orion-Cygnus Arm), a minor spiral arm named after the Orion constellation, not a 'star cluster.' A star cluster (e.g. the real Orion Nebula Cluster) is a compact, gravitationally bound group of stars a few light-years across; the Orion Arm spans roughly 3,500 by 20,000 light-years and holds billions of stars. The claim names the wrong kind of structure, not just an imprecise one.

claim: Only [15%] of stars in the galaxy host planetary systems [00:00]
quote: Only 15% of stars in the galaxy host planetary systems
evidence: Contradicted: a 2012 Berkeley/Caltech microlensing study concluded stars 'are orbited by planets as a rule, rather than the exception,' averaging 1.6 planets per star; NASA's own Kepler-based survey finds roughly 1 in 5 Sun-like stars has an Earth-size planet in the habitable zone alone, before counting giant planets (~20% of stars) or the wider population. Every figure in the literature sits well above 15%.

claim: Mercury has the shortest orbit in the solar system, at about [three Earth months] [00:00]
quote: shortest orbit in the solar system at about three earth months
evidence: 88 days (87.97) / ~30.4-day month ≈ 2.9 months, rounds cleanly to 'about three.' Mercury's orbit is the shortest of the eight planets.

claim: Venus is the hottest planet, with temperatures of up to [867°F] [00:00]
quote: Venus is the hottest planet, with temperatures of up to 867 degrees Fahrenheit
evidence: NASA: Venus's surface is a nearly constant 867°F (464°C), the hottest of any planet, hotter than Mercury despite being farther from the Sun. The figure matches NASA's own number exactly; 'up to' slightly undersells that it barely varies day or night, but the number is right.

claim: Venus's extreme heat is due to [an atmosphere of carbon dioxide and extensive lava flows] [00:00]
quote: due to an atmosphere of carbon dioxide and extensive lava flows
evidence: The proximate cause is a runaway greenhouse effect from Venus's ~96.5% CO2 atmosphere, adding ~500°C of warming on its own — that half of the claim is right. Volcanism's role is indirect: eons of volcanic outgassing built up the CO2 with no ocean to recycle it back into rock, rather than lava itself being a second, ongoing heat source alongside the atmosphere the way the sentence implies. Consistent with the science but the causal chain is compressed.

claim: Mars might have supported life about [3.7 billion years ago], when it had a watery surface and moist atmosphere [01:02]
quote: Mars, might have also supported life about 3.7 billion years ago, when the planet had a watery surface and moist atmosphere
evidence: NASA: Mars could have been habitable as early as 4.48 billion years ago, and evidence of surface liquid water persists to roughly 2-2.5 billion years ago — 3.7 billion years ago falls inside that window, when the atmosphere was denser and warmer. 'Might have supported life' is appropriately hedged; no life has been confirmed, only habitable conditions.

claim: Gas giants [Jupiter, Saturn] are predominantly helium and hydrogen; ice giants [Uranus, Neptune] also contain rock, ice, and a liquid mixture of water, methane, and ammonia [01:02]
quote: The gas giants are predominantly made of helium and hydrogen, and the ice giants also contain rock, ice, and a liquid mixture of water, methane, and ammonia
evidence: Jupiter and Saturn are >90% hydrogen/helium by mass; Uranus and Neptune are ~20% hydrogen/helium with rocky cores and mantles of water, methane and ammonia ('ices') under pressure — matches the claim's composition breakdown.

claim: Saturn's rings are [wide enough to fit between Earth and the Moon] [01:02]
quote: Its signature rings are wide enough to fit between earth and the moon
evidence: NASA Space Place gives the ring system's span as ~400,000 km, comparable to the ~384,000 km average Earth-Moon distance; other estimates put the main rings at 270,000-300,000 km (about three-quarters of that distance). Either way, the comparison is the right order of magnitude.

claim: Saturn's rings are [fairly a kilometer thick] [01:02]
quote: but are fairly a kilometer thick
evidence: Measured thickness is tens of meters, not a kilometer: Britannica puts the main rings at under 100 m thick, and NASA/GSFC's figure is 10-20 m average — roughly 50-100x thinner than claimed. Width-to-thickness ratio runs about 10-20 million to one, the opposite of 'fairly a kilometer.'

claim: Uranus is [the slightly bigger] of the two ice giants, compared with Neptune [01:02]
quote: The slightly bigger of these ice giants
evidence: Uranus's equatorial diameter (~51,118 km) is about 1,500 km larger than Neptune's (~49,528 km) — Uranus is the larger of the two ice giants by diameter, even though Neptune is more massive.

claim: Neptune is the outermost planet in the solar system and [one of the coldest] [02:05]
quote: Neptune, the outermost planet in the solar system and also one of the coldest
evidence: Neptune is the outermost planet since Pluto's 2006 reclassification, and its atmosphere reaches roughly -214°C — among the coldest in the solar system, though Uranus holds the record low at -224°C. The claim only says 'one of the coldest,' which holds; it doesn't claim Neptune is the single coldest.

claim: The largest known object in the asteroid belt is [the dwarf planet Ceres] [02:05]
quote: the largest known object, the dwarf planet Ceres
evidence: NASA: Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, reclassified from asteroid to dwarf planet in 2006.

claim: The Kuiper Belt is home to dwarf planets such as Pluto, and is [the birthplace of many comets] [02:05]
quote: the Kuiper Belt is also home to dwarf planets such as Pluto, and is the birthplace of many comets
evidence: NASA: the Kuiper Belt holds Pluto plus the other recognized dwarf planets in that region (Eris, Makemake, Haumea) and is the source of short-period comets, perturbed inward by Neptune's gravity — matches the claim as stated.

claim: The Oort Cloud is considered [the edge of the solar system] since that is where the sun's gravitational and physical influence ends [02:05]
quote: It is considered the edge of the Solar system since that is where the gravitational and physical influences of the sun end
evidence: NASA: the Oort Cloud 'marks the gravitational edge of the Solar System' — beyond its outer boundary (~100,000 AU), the gravity of other stars starts to dominate over the Sun's. Matches the claim directly.
